l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: King Srênika meets a restrained and concentrated saint at the Mandikukshi Kaitya and learns that worldly wealth and relatives cannot protect a person from suffering. The saint recounts his severe illness in Kausâmbî, his recovery, and his ordination as a houseless monk. He teaches that self-control, careful observance of the great vows, and freedom from sensuality are required to follow the Law of the Nirgranthas. Srênika accepts the teaching, asks forgiveness, and becomes a staunch believer in the Law.

l: The Great Duty of the Nirgranthas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: The Great Duty of the Nirgranthas is preached by the saint as a sermon on protection, self-control, observance of vows, and liberation. It teaches that those who possess virtuous conduct and destroy their Karman will reach the permanent place.

The Nirgranthas are described as following a road requiring strict vows, penance, self-control, and freedom from sinful influences. Those who adopt their Law but act carelessly or pursue sensuality will suffer and fail to attain liberation.

l: King Srênika, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: King Srênika, ruler of Magadha, encounters the saint and initially offers worldly protection and pleasures. After hearing the saint's teaching, he recognizes the meaning of being without protection, asks forgiveness, and becomes a staunch believer in the Law.

The restrained and concentrated saint sits beneath a tree at the Mandikukshi Kaitya and explains that neither relatives nor worldly possessions can protect a person from suffering. He recounts his illness, ordination, and teaching on the great duty of the Nirgranthas.
Kausâmbî is the town where the saint's wealthy father lived. During his childhood there, the saint suffered a severe eye-disease, burning fever, and intense bodily pains.
The Ginas are described as having the highest road, which the self-willed sinner leaves when pursuing pleasure. The wise person is instructed to follow their road.

l: Circle of Births, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: The Circle of Births is described as endless and full of recurring pain. The saint resolves to become a houseless monk if he can escape his great pains and thereby cease acting.

Protection is explained as something not supplied by wealth, rulers, physicians, parents, siblings, or spouses. A person becomes the protector of himself and others through his own conduct, while his own Self is the doer and undoer of misery and happiness.

l: the Law of the Nirgranthas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: The Law of the Nirgranthas is harmed when it is mixed with sensuality, carelessness, forbidden alms, magic, divination, or neglect of vows and self-control. Those who follow it properly can destroy Karman and reach the greatest permanent place.

l: five great vows, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: The great vows must be strictly kept by an ordained monk. Carelessness toward them prevents his fetters from being completely cut off and causes him to fail in the battle of life.

l: the saint's illness, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: The saint's illness included a very bad eye-disease, severe burning fever, and dreadful pains in his eyes, back, heart, and head. Physicians, his family, and his wife could not rid him of the pains, but after he fell asleep they vanished.

l: the saint's ordination, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twentieth Lecture.
s: After his illness disappeared, the saint took leave of his relations and became a houseless monk, calm, restrained, and ceasing to act. Through his ordination he became the protector of himself and of all living beings, whether they move or not.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-First Lecture.
s: The Twenty-First Lecture concerns Samudrapâla, the son of the merchant and Srâvaka Pâlita, who was born at sea and raised in Kampâ. After seeing a condemned man, Samudrapâla understood the consequences of wicked actions, renounced household life, and became a monk. He followed the Law of monks, endured hardships and calamities, and cultivated restraint and detachment. Having annihilated his Karman, he crossed worldly existence and obtained exemption from transmigration.

l: Twenty-First Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-First Lecture.
s: The Twenty-First Lecture tells the story of Samudrapâla, his renunciation of household life, and his practice of the Law of monks. It teaches how restraint, endurance, and detachment lead beyond worldly existence.

Samudrapâla was born at sea to Pâlita’s wife and grew up in comfort in Kampâ. After seeing a condemned man, he became enlightened, entered the state of houselessness, practised the Law of monks, endured calamities, annihilated his Karman, and obtained exemption from transmigration.
Kampâ was the town where Pâlita lived and where Samudrapâla was raised.

Pâlita was a merchant and a Srâvaka who was a disciple of the noble and venerable Mahâvîra. While doing business in Pihunda, he received a merchant’s daughter in marriage and later brought her with him toward Kampâ.

l: Law of monks, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-First Lecture.
s: The Law of monks requires the five great vows: not killing, speaking the truth, not stealing, chastity, and having no property. It also teaches compassion, restraint, endurance, detachment, and the control of the senses.

Monks should endure pleasant and unpleasant conditions, avoid improper replies, remain indifferent to praise and blame, and bear dangers caused by gods, men, or animals without fear. They should control their senses, practise compassion and chastity, and use beds that are not prepared or strewn for their sake.
Calamities may be caused by gods, men, or animals and may be difficult to endure. A steadfast monk bears them without fear, like a stately elephant at the head of the battle.

l: worldly existence, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-First Lecture.
s: Worldly existence is described as an ocean-like Flood to which beings are exposed, along with distress, delusion, fear, and attachment. Samudrapâla crossed it after freeing himself from fetters and annihilating his Karman.
Nirvâna is the path entered by an ascetic who has ceased to act and practises simplicity. Samudrapâla reached exemption from transmigration after following this path.
Karman may be both meritorious and sinful and binds beings to transmigration. Samudrapâla annihilated his Karman and thereby obtained exemption from transmigration.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: This unit concerns Arishtanêmi, his intended marriage to Râgîmatî, and his renunciation after seeing animals prepared for slaughter. Râgîmatî, hearing of his ordination, also renounces and later resists Rathanêmi when he is tempted to pursue her. Both Rathanêmi and Râgîmatî return to the Law, practise severe austerities, become Kêvalins, and reach the highest perfection. The unit teaches that the enlightened turn away from pleasures and maintain self-control.

Rathanêmi sees Râgîmatî naked in a cave, becomes disturbed in mind, and asks her to become his lover. After she rebukes him and urges self-control, he returns to the Law, practises true Sramanahood throughout life, and becomes a Kêvalin who reaches the highest perfection.

Vasudêva is a powerful king of Sauryapura and the father of Râma and Kêsava. He gives Arishtanêmi his blessings after Arishtanêmi plucks out his hair, and later says to Râgîmatî that she should cross the ocean of Samsâra.
Kêsava asks for Râgîmatî in marriage for Arishtanêmi. He travels with the wedding procession and returns to Dvârakâ after Arishtanêmi renounces.
Samudravigaya is a powerful king of Sauryapura and the father of Arishtanêmi and Rathanêmi.

Arishtanêmi is the son of Samudravigaya and Sivâ, the saviour of the world, and the lord of ascetics. While travelling to marry Râgîmatî, he sees animals destined for slaughter, renounces, plucks out his hair, and later becomes a Kêvalin who reaches the highest perfection.

Râgîmatî is the virtuous daughter of an excellent king and the intended bride of Arishtanêmi. After hearing of his ordination, she renounces, induces others to enter the order, and later defends her vows against Rathanêmi; after severe austerities she becomes a Kêvalin and reaches the highest perfection.
Arishtanêmi leaves Dvârakâ on an excellent palankin and ascends mount Raivataka. After honouring him, Râma, Kêsava, the Dasârhas, and many people return to Dvârakâ.
Raivataka is the mountain Arishtanêmi ascends after leaving Dvârakâ. His renunciation takes place in a park there, and Râgîmatî later travels toward the mountain.

l: marriage of Arishtanêmi and Râgîmatî, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: Kêsava seeks Râgîmatî in marriage for Arishtanêmi, and preparations are made for the wedding. The marriage does not take place because Arishtanêmi renounces after seeing animals kept for slaughter.

l: Arishtanêmi's renunciation, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: Arishtanêmi renounces when he learns that animals are being kept to provide food at his wedding. He leaves Dvârakâ, ascends mount Raivataka, plucks out his hair, and enters the order.

l: Râgîmatî's renunciation, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: Râgîmatî renounces after hearing that Arishtanêmi has become ordained. She cuts off her hair, enters the order, and induces many relations and servants to enter it as well.

l: ascetic practice, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: Rathanêmi and Râgîmatî practise true Sramanahood and severe austerities throughout life. Their practice leads them to become Kêvalins and to reach the highest perfection.
Râgîmatî maintains self-control and her vows when Rathanêmi tempts her. Her words lead Rathanêmi to return to the Law, after which he protects his thoughts, words, and acts and subdues his senses.

l: the highest perfection, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Second Lecture.
s: Rathanêmi and Râgîmatî reach the highest perfection after becoming Kêvalins and completely annihilating their Karman.
Rathanêmi urges Râgîmatî to enjoy pleasures before entering the path of the Ginas. Râgîmatî rejects this, and the unit teaches that the enlightened turn from pleasures.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: This unit concerns the meeting of Kêsi, disciple of Pârsva, and Gautama, disciple of Vardhamâna, at Srâvastî. They resolve questions about the differences between the Law of Pârsva and the Law of Vardhamâna, including four versus five vows and clothing rules. Gautama explains metaphors for conquering the passions and senses, destroying fetters and love of existence, extinguishing the fire of the passions, controlling the mind, following the right path, and reaching Nirvâna. Kêsi accepts the Law of the five vows, and the assembly praises both teachers.

Pârsva is described as a Gina, Arhat, prophet of the Law, and thoroughly enlightened and omniscient. His famous disciple is Kêsi, and the Law he taught recognises four vows and allows an under and upper garment.

Kêsi is a young Sramana and famous disciple of Pârsva who has mastered the sciences and right conduct, possesses Sruta and Avadhi knowledge, and arrives at Srâvastî. He questions Gautama about the two Laws and, after his doubts are resolved, adopts the Law of the five vows.
Vardhamâna is the Gina and prophet of the Law known throughout the world. His famous disciple is Gautama, and the Law he taught enjoins five vows and forbids clothes for a monk.

Gautama is a famous disciple of Vardhamâna who has mastered the sciences and right conduct, knows the twelve Aṅgas, and arrives at Srâvastî. He answers Kêsi’s questions, explaining the differences between the two Laws and the means of overcoming spiritual dangers.
Srâvastî is the town to which both Kêsi and Gautama arrive while wandering from village to village. Its district contains the Tinduka park and Kôshthaka park.

l: Tinduka park, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Tinduka park in the district of Srâvastî is where Kêsi takes up residence. Gautama later goes there with his pupils to meet Kêsi, and Kêsi adopts the Law of the five vows there.

l: the Law of Pârsva, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Law of Pârsva recognises four vows and allows an under and upper garment. Gautama explains that its difference from the Law of Vardhamâna arose because the capacities of beings differed across the ages.

l: the Law of Vardhamâna, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Law of Vardhamâna enjoins five vows and forbids clothes for a monk. Kêsi adopts this Law after Gautama resolves his doubts.

l: the four vows, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The four vows are recognised by the Law taught by Pârsva. They are presented as pursuing the same end as the five vows.

l: the five vows, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The five vows are enjoined by the Law taught by Vardhamâna. Kêsi sincerely adopts this Law after the meeting with Gautama.

l: the Tîrthakaras, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Tîrthakaras fixed what is necessary for carrying out the Law by their superior knowledge. They introduced various outward marks so religious people could be recognised, while teaching that knowledge, faith, and right conduct cause final liberation.

l: the disciples of Kêsi and Gautama, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The disciples of Kêsi and Gautama control themselves, practise austerities, possess virtues, and protect their Self. They wonder which Law, conduct, and doctrines are right, prompting Kêsi and Gautama to meet.

l: clothing rules for monks, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The clothing rules differ between the two Laws: the Law of Pârsva allows an under and upper garment, while the Law of Vardhamâna forbids clothes for a monk. Gautama explains that outward marks are useful for religious life and recognition but are not the true causes of final liberation.

l: knowledge, faith, and right conduct, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: Knowledge, faith, and right conduct are taught to be the true causes of final liberation, rather than outward marks.
The Self is identified as the one invincible foe. Gautama says he has regularly vanquished it together with the four cardinal passions and the five senses.

l: four cardinal passions, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The cardinal passions are anger, pride, deceit, and greed. Together with the Self, they form five foes that Gautama says he has vanquished.
The five senses are counted among the ten foes. Gautama says he has regularly vanquished them along with the Self and the cardinal passions.

l: the ten foes, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The ten foes consist of the Self, the four cardinal passions, and the five senses. Gautama explains that by vanquishing one and then five, he has vanquished all ten.
Fetters bind living beings. Gautama says that he has cut off and destroyed all fetters by the right means and is therefore set free; love, hatred, and attachment are described as fetters.

l: love of existence, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: Love of existence is the dreadful plant that grows in the innermost heart and brings forth dreadful fruit. Gautama says he has torn it out completely with its roots and therefore lives pleasantly.

l: the fire of the passions, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The fire of the passions burns embodied beings. Gautama says it is extinguished by knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances, which he compares to water.

l: knowledge, virtuous life, and penances, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: Knowledge, a virtuous life, and penances are the water that extinguishes the fire of the passions. Gautama says that sprinkled with the drops of knowledge, the fire does not burn him.

l: the mind, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The mind is compared to an unruly, dreadful, bad horse. Gautama governs it by the discipline of the Law and the bridle of knowledge so that it keeps to the right path.

l: the right path, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The right path is the path taught by the Ginas and is described as the most excellent path. Gautama knows both the right and wrong paths and therefore does not go astray.

l: the flood of old age and death, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The flood of old age and death carries away living beings. The Law is described as an island, firm ground, refuge, and excellent shelter that is not inundated by this flood.

l: the Law as refuge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Law is the island and firm ground that provides refuge and excellent shelter from the flood of old age and death.
The body is compared to a boat crossing the ocean of the Circle of Births. A boat that leaks will not reach the opposite shore, while one that does not leak will reach it.
Life is compared to the sailor of the boat that crosses the ocean of the Circle of Births.

l: Circle of Births, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The Circle of Births is compared to an ocean crossed by the great sages. The omniscient Gina and the great sages bring an end to this cycle.

l: the omniscient Gina, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The omniscient Gina is compared to the spotless sun that illuminates the whole world of living beings. He has put an end to the Circle of Births and brings light to the world.

Nirvâna is freedom from pain, perfection, and a safe, happy, and quiet place. It is eternal and difficult to approach, and the sages who reach it are free from sorrow and have ended the stream of existence.

l: the meeting of Kêsi and Gautama, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Third Lecture.
s: The meeting of Kêsi and Gautama takes place in the Tinduka park at Srâvastî. Gautama resolves Kêsi’s doubts about the two Laws and spiritual practice, after which Kêsi adopts the Law of the five vows and knowledge and virtuous conduct are brought to eminence.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Fourth Lecture explains the Samitis and Guptis, the eight articles of the creed. It describes five Samitis governing walking, speech, begging, handling necessary articles, and bodily waste, along with three Guptis governing mind, speech, and body. It sets out how a well-disciplined monk should practice these disciplines to avoid harm and sinful conduct. The unit concludes that applying them leads beyond the Circle of Births.

l: Twenty-Fourth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Fourth Lecture concerns the Samitis and Guptis and explains their place in the creed.

l: five Samitis, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The Samitis are five disciplines concerning walking, speech, begging, handling necessary articles, and disposing of bodily waste. In their wider application, the term Samiti includes the three Guptis.
The Guptis are disciplines of mind, speech, and body that prevent sinful conduct. They concern preventing harmful desires, thoughts, speech, and bodily actions.
The creed has eight articles, consisting of five Samitis and three Guptis. The eight Samitis are said to comprehend the whole creed taught by the Ginas and set forth in the twelve Aṅgas.
The îryâ-samiti requires going by paths trodden by men, beasts, and carts while looking carefully to avoid causing the death of any living creature.
The bhâshâ-samiti requires gentle, salutary, sweet, and righteous speech. A well-disciplined monk should use blameless and concise speech at the proper time.
The êshanâ-samiti governs receiving alms in a manner that avoids the forty-two faults that are laid down.
The âdâna-samiti governs receiving and keeping things necessary for religious exercises after carefully examining them.
The ukkâra-samiti governs performing the operations of nature in an unfrequented place. The place should meet various conditions that support self-control and avoid harm to living beings.

The mano-gupti prevents the mind from wandering in the forest of sensual pleasures by employing it in contemplation, study, and similar activities. It also prevents harmful desires and thoughts concerning acts that cause misery or destruction to living beings.

The vâg-gupti prevents the tongue from saying bad things by practices such as a vow of silence. It also prevents speech expressing harmful desires or concerning acts that cause misery or destruction to living beings.

The kâya-gupti puts the body in an immovable posture, as in Kâyôtsarga. It prevents the body, in standing, sitting, lying down, jumping, going, and using its organs, from expressing harmful desires or causing misery or destruction to living beings.

The well-disciplined monk walks purely with regard to cause, time, road, and effort, and he avoids the eight faults of speech. He carefully practices the Samitis and Guptis in walking, begging, handling articles, disposing of waste, and controlling mind, speech, and body.

Walking should be pure in respect to cause, time, road, and effort. A monk should look with his eyes, attend to the space of a yuga, remain attentive as long as he walks, and focus on his walk and body while avoiding the objects of sense.

Begging requires avoiding faults in the search for, receiving, and use of food, articles of use, and lodging. A zealous monk should avoid faults caused by the giver or receiver, faults inherent in receiving, and four faults in using the articles received.

l: religious exercise, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The five Samitis are prescribed for the practice of the religious life, while the Guptis prevent everything sinful. A sage who thoroughly practices their essence will soon get beyond the Circle of Births.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fifth Lecture.
s: Gayaghôsha, a Brâhmana and houseless sage, comes to Benares and challenges Vigayaghôsha and the assembled priests about the essentials of the Vêdas, sacrifice, heavenly bodies, dharma, and true Brâhmanahood. He teaches that true spiritual status depends on conduct, chastity, knowledge, penance, non-violence, truthfulness, non-attachment, and freedom from Karman rather than outward marks or ritual learning. Vigayaghôsha accepts the teaching, enters the monastic order, and together with Gayaghôsha annihilates Karman through self-control and penance, reaching the highest perfection.

Gayaghôsha is a famous Brâhmana who performs the yamas, subdues his senses, and wanders from village to village. At Benares he refuses to be angered when denied alms, teaches Vigayaghôsha and the assembled priests about true Brâhmanahood and liberation, and urges Vigayaghôsha to enter the order. He later annihilates his Karman through self-control and penance and reaches the highest perfection.

Vigayaghôsha is a Brâhmana versed in the Vêdas who offers a sacrifice at Benares and initially refuses alms to Gayaghôsha. After questioning Gayaghôsha and hearing his teaching, he assents to it, praises his knowledge, enters the order, and annihilates his Karman through self-control and penance.

A Brâhmana is not truly defined by public honor, sacred syllables, ritual learning, or outward observances. The true Brâhmana is free from worldly attachment, love, hatred, fear, falsehood, taking what is not given, sensual desire, greed, and householder ties, and is known by the wise through his conduct.

The priests claim that Vêda-versed, chaste, sacrificially learned priests should receive food and all they desire. Gayaghôsha teaches that ignorant priests who merely pretend to know sacrifice and hide behind study and penance cannot thereby save themselves or others.

l: the Vêdas, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fifth Lecture.
s: The most essential subject in the Vêdas is said to be the agnihôtra. Gayaghôsha also teaches that mere knowledge of the Vêdas does not make a person a true Brâhmana or provide liberation.
The most essential element of sacrifice is its purpose. The binding of animals, all the Vêdas, and sacrifices are described as causes of sin that cannot save the sinner because Karman is powerful.

The best of dharmas is identified with that of Kâsyapa, or Rishabha. True dharma is also expressed through equanimity, chastity, knowledge, penance, non-violence, truthfulness, non-possession, and freedom from attachment.

l: the monastic order, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fifth Lecture.
s: Entering the monastic order requires giving up worldly attachment and former connections and taking delight in noble words. Gayaghôsha urges Vigayaghôsha to enter it at once so that he will not continue drifting on the dreadful ocean of Samsâra.
A pious, self-subduing ascetic who reduces his flesh and blood and reaches Nirvâna is called a true Brâhmana.

Karman is described as very powerful, so animal sacrifice, Vêdas, and sacrifices cannot save the sinner from its effects. Those who love pleasure become fastened to Karman, while the passionless do not; Gayaghôsha and Vigayaghôsha annihilate their Karman through self-control and penance.

Pleasure is compared to glue because those who are attached to it become soiled and must wander in Samsâra. Those who are not given to pleasure are not soiled by it, like a dry clod of clay that does not stick to a wall.
Samsâra is described as a dreadful ocean whose eddies are dangers. Attachment to pleasure causes beings to continue wandering in it, while freedom from pleasure leads to liberation.

l: the true sacrifice, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fifth Lecture.
s: The teaching presents the true sacrifice as spiritual conduct rather than outward ritual. It consists in qualities such as self-control, chastity, knowledge, penance, non-violence, truthfulness, non-possession, and freedom from attachment and Karman.

l: the highest perfection, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Fifth Lecture.
s: The highest perfection is reached by Gayaghôsha and Vigayaghôsha after they annihilate their Karman through self-control and penance.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Sixth Lecture.
s: The lecture explains the correct behaviour of monks, called sâmâkârî, as the discipline that frees them from misery and helps them cross Samsâra. It defines the tenfold correct behaviour and prescribes the monks’ duties during the four divisions of the day and night, including study, meditation, begging-tour, inspection, confession, and Kâyôtsarga. It also gives rules for inspecting possessions, protecting living beings, observing the Guru, and performing Kâla-pratikramana and the Pratikramana Sûtra. The unit concludes that many souls have crossed Samsâra by practising this correct behaviour.

l: correct behaviour, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Correct behaviour, or sâmâkârî, causes freedom from misery. By practising it, many souls have crossed Samsâra.
Samsâra is described as an ocean from which Nirgranthas and many souls have crossed through correct behaviour.
The Nirgranthas have crossed the ocean of Samsâra by practising correct behaviour.

Monks must practise the tenfold correct behaviour and fulfil prescribed duties throughout the day and night. They study, meditate, beg when permitted, inspect their possessions, confess transgressions, and perform Kâyôtsarga.

l: tenfold correct behaviour, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Sixth Lecture.
s: The tenfold correct behaviour consists of âvasyikâ, naishêdhikî, âprikkhanâ, pratiprikkhanâ, khandanâ, ikkhâkâra, mithyâkâra, tathâkâra, abhyutthâna, and upasampad.
Monks pay reverence to the Guru at prescribed times, ask what work or study they should undertake, and seek absolution after confessing transgressions.
The day and night are each divided into four Paurushî. Their length varies by season, and each division is assigned duties such as study, meditation, begging-tour, or leaving off sleep.

A monk divides the day into four Paurushî and fulfils his duties in each: study, meditation, begging-tour, and study again. He also performs inspections, confession, Kâla-pratikramana, and Kâyôtsarga during the day.

A monk divides the night into four Paurushî and uses them for study, meditation, leaving off sleep, and study again. He performs night inspection, Kâla-pratikramana, Kâyôtsarga, reflection, and confession.

Study is undertaken during the first and fourth Paurushî of the day and the first and fourth Paurushî of the night. A monk should study without allowing pains to affect him and should not wake householders.
Meditation is undertaken during the second Paurushî of the day and the second Paurushî of the night. Food may be begged so that a monk can meditate on the Law.
The begging-tour occurs in the third Paurushî of the day. Food and drink may be sought to prevent illness, serve the Guru, follow walking and self-control rules, save life, or meditate on the Law.

Monks inspect and clean their possessions after sunrise, inspect their almsbowl and lodging, and inspect the place for discharging excrements and urine. Careful inspection protects living beings, while careless inspection injures them.

l: Living Beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Sixth Lecture.
s: The six kinds of living beings are earth-bodies, water-bodies, fire-bodies, wind-bodies, plants, and animals. Careful inspection protects them from injury.

A monk performs Kâla-pratikramana at prescribed points, including after the day's study and before the night's proper activities. It is not performed during the inspection of the almsbowl in the last quarter of the first Paurushî.
Monks perform Kâyôtsarga during the day and night without allowing themselves to be affected by pains. After it, they reflect on and confess transgressions concerning knowledge, faith, and conduct.

l: Pratikramana Sûtra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Sixth Lecture.
s: After reflecting on transgressions, a monk recites the Pratikramana Sûtra and thereby annihilates his sins before reverencing the Guru and performing further Kâyôtsarga.
At the end of the night duties, a monk considers which austerities he will undertake. He then practises the austerities he has decided upon and praises the perfected saints.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Seventh Lecture, titled The Bad Bullocks, concerns the reflections of Garga, a Sthavira and Ganadhara. Garga compares crossing a wilderness by car and crossing the Samsâra through religious exercise, then compares bad bullocks with bad pupils yoked to the car of the Law. The unit describes the unruly behavior of bad bullocks and the lack of zeal, objections, disobedience, and dispersal of bad pupils. Garga ultimately leaves the lazy donkeys and practises severe austerities.

l: Twenty-Seventh Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Seventh Lecture presents Garga’s reflections on bad bullocks and bad pupils. It concludes with Garga leaving the lazy donkeys and practising severe austerities.

l: The Bad Bullocks, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: The Bad Bullocks is the title of the lecture. It concerns comparisons between bad bullocks and bad pupils.

Garga is a Sthavira and Ganadhara and the learned sage who makes reflections about cars, religious exercise, bad bullocks, and bad pupils. After becoming disheartened by bad pupils, he leaves the lazy donkeys and practises severe austerities.
A car is used to cross a wilderness. When bad bullocks are put before it, they may cause exhaustion, vexation, damage to the goad, the yoke, the pin, or the rope, and may run off.

l: religious exercise, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: Religious exercise is compared to a car in which one crosses the Samsâra.
The Samsâra is crossed by one who rides, as it were, in the car of religious exercise.

l: bad bullocks, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: Bad bullocks may bite or wound their mate, break the pin or yoke, leave the road, fall down, sit or lie down, jump or caper, pursue a young cow, attack, go backward, stand still, run at full speed, rend the rope, and break loose. They are compared with bad pupils yoked to the car of the Law.

l: bad pupils, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Seventh Lecture.
s: Bad pupils break down through want of zeal, attach importance to success, fare, comfort, or anger, and may be averse to begging or afraid of insults. They make objections, oppose superiors, avoid errands, act disobediently, and disperse after being instructed, admitted into the order, and nourished.
The Law is described as a car to which bad pupils are yoked, as bad bullocks are put before a car.
Garga decides to leave the lazy donkeys and practise severe austerities. He then wanders about on the earth, leading a virtuous life.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Eighth Lecture.
s: The unit explains the road to final deliverance taught by the Ginas, which consists of right knowledge, faith, conduct, and austerities. It describes five kinds of knowledge, six kinds of substances, the nine truths, and ten causes by which faith is produced. It teaches that right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerities are mutually connected and lead beings toward beatitude and perfection. Great sages destroy their Karman through control and austerities and proceed to final deliverance.
Final deliverance is the goal reached through right knowledge, faith, conduct, and austerities. Without deliverance there is no perfection.

l: The Road of Penance, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Eighth Lecture.
s: The road to final deliverance is taught by the Ginas and depends on four causes: right knowledge, faith, conduct, and austerities. Beings who follow it obtain beatitude.
The Ginas possess the best knowledge and have taught the road to final deliverance, the six kinds of substances, and the nine truths.

l: right knowledge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Eighth Lecture.
s: Right knowledge is one of the four causes of final deliverance and is fivefold: Sruta, Âbhinibôdhika, Avadhi, Manahparyâya, and Kêvala. Without right faith there is no right knowledge, and without right knowledge there is no virtuous conduct.

Faith is one of the four causes of final deliverance and is produced by ten causes, including nature, instruction, command, study of the Sûtras, comprehension of sacred lore, religious exercise, and the Law. Right belief depends on acquaintance with truth, devotion to those who know the truth, and avoidance of schismatical and heretical tenets.

Conduct is one of the four causes of final deliverance and produces the destruction of all Karman. It is fivefold, including the avoidance of everything sinful, initiation of a novice, purity from peculiar austerities, reduction of desire, and annihilation of sinfulness according to the precepts of the Arhats.

Austerities are one of the four causes of final deliverance and are twofold, external and internal, each being sixfold. Through austerities one reaches purity and destroys Karman together with control.
Substance is the substrate of qualities, while qualities are inherent in one substance. Dharma, Adharma, space, time, matter, and souls are the six kinds of substances.
Souls are one of the six kinds of substances and exist in an infinite number. Their characteristics include knowledge, faith, conduct, austerities, energy, and realisation of their developments.

l: the nine truths, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Eighth Lecture.
s: The nine truths are soul, inanimate things, the binding of the soul by Karman, merit, demerit, that which causes the soul to be affected by sins, prevention of that cause by watchfulness, annihilation of Karman, and final deliverance. He who truly believes their teaching possesses righteousness.

l: annihilation of Karman, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Eighth Lecture.
s: Annihilation of Karman is one of the nine truths and is included in the conduct that produces the destruction of all Karman. Great sages destroy their Karman through control and austerities.
Karman binds the soul and is connected with merit, demerit, and the causes by which the soul is affected by sins. It is destroyed through conduct, control, and austerities.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Ninth Lecture, called The Exertion in Righteousness, records Sudharman’s discourse from the venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra. It explains seventy-three practices and virtues through which the soul develops faith, discipline, knowledge, conduct, renunciation, and control. These practices destroy or prevent Karman, lead the soul beyond Samsâra, and culminate in pure meditation, perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, and final beatitude.

l: Twenty-Ninth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: The Twenty-Ninth Lecture concerns The Exertion in Righteousness and explains the results of seventy-three practices, virtues, forms of renunciation, disciplines, and stages of spiritual progress.

l: The Exertion in Righteousness, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: The Exertion in Righteousness is the subject of Mahâvîra’s lecture. It teaches how exertion in the Law destroys Karman and brings the soul to perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, and final beatitude.
Mahâvîra, the venerable Ascetic of the Kasyapa Gôtra, delivered the lecture called The Exertion in Righteousness.
Sudharman reports that he heard this discourse from the venerable Mahâvîra.

The Ginas prescribe the precepts according to which creatures practise the teachings. Adoration of the twenty-four Ginas purifies faith, and their proclaimed Law is to be practised in this world and the next.

The soul obtains faith, discipline, knowledge, conduct, concentration, control, and freedom from passions through the practices described. By destroying Karman and completing pure meditation, it obtains perfection, enlightenment, deliverance, and final beatitude.

The Law inspires longing for liberation, leads to indifference toward worldly pleasures, and guides the soul toward houseless life and freedom from pain. Study, recital, discourse, and sincere practice of the Law destroy ignorance and Karman.

Longing for liberation produces an intense desire of the Law and helps the soul abandon wrong belief and destructive passions. Exertion directed toward liberation ultimately leads the soul beyond Samsâra.
Perfection is obtained when the soul destroys Karman, ceases activity, and completes the required spiritual practices. The soul then ends all misery.
Enlightenment follows the destruction of Karman and the attainment of absolute knowledge and faith. The perfected soul obtains enlightenment together with deliverance and final beatitude.

l: final deliverance, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: Deliverance is attained after the soul destroys the remaining Karman and rises to the highest Akâsa. It accompanies perfection, enlightenment, and final beatitude.

l: eternal beatitude, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: Final beatitude is obtained when the soul has destroyed Karman, ended worldly existence, and developed into its natural form. It is described as the end of all misery.

Karman is acquired through sinful, uncontrolled, deluded, or worldly activity and is prevented or destroyed through discipline, study, austerities, renunciation, concentration, and pure meditation. The soul ultimately annihilates the eightfold Karman and becomes exempt from Karman.
Samsâra is the beginningless and endless fourfold forest of worldly existence. The soul crosses it by abandoning worldly undertakings, destroying Karman, and following the road to perfection.

Houseless monks abandon household life, practise discipline and the Law, and endure bodily and mental difficulties. Through conduct, renunciation, control, and austerities, they can destroy Karman and attain final liberation.

The Guru receives confession and repentance, and obedience and reverence toward the Guru produce discipline, prevent blameable conduct, and support spiritual progress. Service, praise, devotion, and respect toward the Guru lead to commendable results.
Samvêga is longing for liberation. It produces an intense desire of the Law, helps destroy anger, pride, deceit, and greed, and supports the attainment of right faith and eventual perfection.

l: pure meditation, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Twenty-Ninth Lecture.
s: Pure meditation is the final stage in which the soul ceases the functions of mind, speech, body, and breathing. During the final pure meditation, it annihilates the four remaining kinds of Karman and rises to its natural form.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: The Thirtieth Lecture, called The Road of Penance, explains how a monk destroys Karman acquired through love and hatred. It describes how abstaining from prescribed actions and possessing specified virtues makes the soul free from Âsravas. It classifies austerities as external and internal, detailing their six kinds and their subdivisions. It teaches that faithfully performing both kinds of austerities leads to release from the Circle of Births.

l: Thirtieth Lecture, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: The Thirtieth Lecture explains the Road of Penance and how a monk destroys Karman acquired by love and hatred through austerities.

l: The Road of Penance, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: The Road of Penance teaches the practices by which a monk stops the influx of bad Karman and annihilates Karman acquired in millions of births.

A monk becomes free from Âsravas by abstaining from destroying life, lying, taking what is not given, sexual indulgence, property, and eating at night. By performing external and internal austerities, the monk can be thoroughly released from the Circle of Births.
The soul becomes free from Âsravas through the prescribed abstentions, the five Samitis, the three Guptis, freedom from passions, subduing the senses, vanquishing conceit, and avoiding delusions.
Karman acquired by a monk in millions of births is annihilated by austerities when there is no influx of bad Karman.

l: bad Karman, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: Bad Karman is stopped by prescribed abstentions and virtues; without its influx, austerities gradually destroy the Karman previously acquired by a monk.

l: love and hatred, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: Love and hatred are identified as the causes through which the monk acquired the Karman that austerities destroy.

l: external austerities, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirtieth Lecture.
s: Austerities are of two kinds, external and internal, with six kinds in each group. Faithfully performing both kinds of austerities leads to release from the Circle of Births.

Âsravas cease for the soul through abstention from the six specified actions and through possessing the five Samitis and three Guptis, freedom from passions, subduing the senses, vanquishing conceit, and avoiding delusions.

Fasting is an external austerity of two kinds: temporary fasting and fasting which precedes and ends with death. Temporary fasting has six forms, while fasting before death is classified according to bodily motion and whether relief or leaving the chosen place is allowed.

Abstinence is an external austerity observed with regard to substance, place, time, state of mind, and development. It includes taking less food, restricting the places or times for collecting alms, accepting alms under specified conditions, and following the enumerated particulars.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-First Lecture.
s: The unit concerns the mode of life that benefits the soul and enables souls to cross the ocean of Samsâra. It teaches that one should desist from neglect of self-control and practise self-control. A monk avoids love, hatred, harmful acts, calamities, sinful meditations, and many listed causes of bondage, while exerting himself in vows, duties, virtues, and other prescribed points. A clever monk who follows these teachings will soon be thoroughly released from the Circle of Births.

l: mode of life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-First Lecture.
s: The mode of life benefits the soul. By practising it, many souls have crossed the ocean of Samsâra.
The soul benefits from the declared mode of life. Many souls have crossed the ocean of Samsâra by practising it.
Samsâra is described as an ocean that many souls have crossed through practising the beneficial mode of life.
Self-control should be practised, while neglect of self-control should be avoided.

A monk avoids love and hatred, harmful, conceited, and delusive acts, calamities, sinful meditations, and many other listed faults. He exerts himself with regard to vows, senses, duties, virtues, and other prescribed points; a clever monk who does so will soon be thoroughly released from the Circle of Births.
Love and hatred produce bad Karman. A monk who always avoids them will not stand within the circle of transmigration.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: The unit explains how a Sramana may attain final deliverance from beginningless misery through true knowledge, avoidance of ignorance and delusion, and destruction of love and hatred. It teaches that desire, greed, Karman, and birth and death arise in a chain rooted in delusion, while discipline, seclusion, proper food, study, and meditation support righteousness. The text warns that attachment or aversion to pleasures and sensory objects produces passions, suffering, wrongdoing, and further Karman. A dispassionate person becomes free from these obstructions, knows and sees all things, and ultimately obtains beatitude.

l: final deliverance, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: Final deliverance is reached through true knowledge, avoidance of ignorance and delusion, and destruction of love and hatred. It is described as nothing but bliss.
Misery arises from birth and death and from attachment, aversion, desire, and sensory pleasures. It ceases when delusion ceases, and the dispassionate eventually become free from all misery.

l: right knowledge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: True knowledge is taught as a means to final deliverance. The dispassionate person who performs all duties removes the obstructions to right knowledge.

l: ignorance and delusion, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: Ignorance and delusion are to be avoided because delusion gives rise to desire and Karman. When delusion is absent, misery ceases.

l: love and hatred, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: Love and hatred are to be destroyed as causes of bondage and misery. They arise through attachment or aversion to pleasant and unpleasant objects.

Desire is called an origin of delusion, while delusion is also called an origin of desire. Desire ceases with the absence of greed, and the desire for pleasures becomes extinct when sensory objects are no longer desired.
Greed ceases when property is absent. When desire becomes violent, greed leads a person to take another's property, increasing deceit and falsehood without removing misery.
Karman is said to originate in delusion and to cause love and hatred. It is the root of birth and death, and the dispassionate person removes the Karman that obstructs righteousness.

l: birth and death, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: Birth and death are rooted in Karman and are called misery. The teaching presents freedom from this cycle as part of final deliverance.

A Sramana seeking righteousness should serve Gurus and old teachers, study, ponder the Sûtras, eat the proper quantity of allowed food, choose a virtuous companion, and live suitably for seclusion. He should restrain his senses, avoid sensual objects and women, and remain indifferent to pleasant and unpleasant things.

Righteousness is sought by the Sramana through austerities, study, self-control, proper food, suitable companionship, and seclusion. The dispassionate person who performs all duties removes obstructions to righteousness.

Pleasures produce misery and attachment, even though they may appear beautiful or pleasant. A person who seeks liberation should not fix his thoughts on pleasant sensory objects or turn his mind toward unpleasant ones.
The senses are strengthened by unrestricted eating, and their fires are not extinguished when a person eats as he wishes. Their objects cause pain to passionate people, but not to the dispassionate.

Women are presented as a serious difficulty for a man seeking liberation and chastity. A Sramana should not watch, remember, praise, or long for women's forms, beauty, laughter, gestures, glances, or other attractions, and should not stay in a house inhabited by women.

The Samsâra is feared by one who longs for liberation and follows the Law. A person may remain in the Samsâra without being affected by its succession of pains if he is indifferent to sensory objects.

Colour attracts the eye and becomes a cause of love when pleasant and hatred when unpleasant. Passion for colour leads to ruin, violence, dissatisfaction, greed, and misery, whereas indifference to colour frees a person from sorrow.

l: the mind, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Second Lecture.
s: The mind of one who lives in unfrequented lodgings, eats low food, and subdues the senses is protected from Love. Objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate people, while perfect indifference arises when the mind recognizes the vanity of all desires.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Third Lecture.
s: The lecture explains the Nature of Karman and the eight kinds of Karman by which the soul turns round and round in the Circle of Births. It describes their subdivisions, including the forms of obstruction to right knowledge and right faith, pleasure and pain, delusion, life duration, individuality, Gôtra, and prevention of progress toward eternal bliss. It also states their numbers of atoms, spatial extent, durations, and development. A wise man should learn these subdivisions and strive to prevent and destroy them.

The Nature of Karman concerns the eight kinds of Karman bound by which the soul turns round and round in the Circle of Births. Their subdivisions, atoms, places, durations, and development are explained.
The soul turns round and round in the Circle of Births while bound by the eight kinds of Karman. Karman binds the whole soul in all its parts in every possible way.

l: Circle of Births, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Third Lecture.
s: The Circle of Births is where the soul turns round and round because it is bound by Karman.
Gñânâvaranîya acts as an obstruction to right knowledge. Its obstruction is fivefold, concerning Sruta, Âbhinibôdhika, Avadhigñâna, Manahparyâya, and Kêvala knowledge.

Darsanâvaranîya acts as an obstruction to right faith. Its nine kinds include sleep, activity, very deep sleep, a high degree of activity, deep-rooted greed, and faith in specified objects of knowledge.
Vêdanîya leads to experiencing pleasure or pain. It is twofold, and both pleasure and pain have many subdivisions.

Môhanîya leads to delusion and is twofold as referring to faith and conduct. Its faith-related forms are right faith, wrong faith, and faith partly right and partly wrong; its conduct-related forms concern the four cardinal passions and other feelings.

Âyuhkarman determines the length of life. It is fourfold as referring to denizens of hell, brute creation, men, and gods, with a longest duration of thirty-three Krores of Krores of Sâgarôpamâs and a shortest duration of a part of a muhûrta.
Antarâya prevents one's entrance on the path that leads to eternal bliss. It is fivefold as preventing gifts, profit, momentary enjoyment, continuous enjoyment, and power.

l: right knowledge, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Third Lecture.
s: Right knowledge is obstructed by Gñânâvaranîya. The obstruction includes knowledge derived from the sacred books, perception, supernatural knowledge, knowledge of the thoughts of other people, and the highest, unlimited knowledge.
Right faith is obstructed by Darsanâvaranîya. Môhanîya also concerns faith, including right faith, wrong faith, and faith partly right and partly wrong.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The unit concerns the six Lêsyâs produced by Karman and describes their names, colours, tastes, smells, touches, degrees, character, varieties, duration, results, and life. The black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs arise from wicked and uncontrolled habits, while the red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs arise from increasing discipline, calm, and observance of the Law. Their durations vary across hell, animals, men, and gods, and their degrees have three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, or two hundred and forty-three divisions. The bad Lêsyâs bring souls into miserable courses of life, while the good Lêsyâs bring them into happy courses of life.
Lêsyâs are six in number and are named black, blue, grey, red, yellow, and white. This unit describes their qualities, degrees, varieties, durations, results, and conditions at birth.
Karman produces the six Lêsyâs.

l: black Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The black Lêsyâ has the colour of a rain-cloud, a buffalo's horn, Rishtaka, or the eye of the wagtail. It develops in a person ruled by the five Âsravas, lacking the three Guptis, injuring living beings, and acting cruelly and violently; it is one of the lowest Lêsyâs and brings the soul into miserable courses of life.

l: blue Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The blue Lêsyâ has the colour of the blue Asôka, the tail of the Kasha, or lapis lazuli. It develops in a person marked by envy, anger, want of self-control, deceit, greed, hatred, carelessness, and sinful undertakings; it is one of the lowest Lêsyâs and brings the soul into miserable courses of life.

l: grey Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The grey Lêsyâ has the colour of the flower of Atasî, the feathers of the Kôkila, or the collar of pigeons. It develops in a dishonest, base, deceitful, heretical, hurtful, thieving, and jealous person; it is one of the lowest Lêsyâs and brings the soul into miserable courses of life.

l: red Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The red Lêsyâ has the colour of vermilion, the rising sun, or the bill of a parrot. It develops in a humble, steadfast, disciplined, restrained person who loves and keeps the Law; it is one of the good Lêsyâs and brings the soul into happy courses of life.

l: yellow Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The yellow Lêsyâ has the colour of orpiment, turmeric, or the flowers of Sana and Asana. It develops in a calm and self-controlled person with little anger, pride, deceit, and greed; it is one of the good Lêsyâs and brings the soul into happy courses of life.

l: white Lêsyâ, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: The white Lêsyâ has the colour of a conch-shell, the aṅka-stone, Kunda-flowers, flowing milk, silver, or a necklace of pearls. It develops in a person who meditates on the Law and truth, practises the Samitis and Guptis, and subdues the senses; it is one of the good Lêsyâs and brings the soul into happy courses of life.

The Law is loved, kept, and meditated on by persons who develop the red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs. Meditation on the Law and truth, together with practice of the Samitis and Guptis, is associated with the white Lêsyâ.

l: miserable courses of life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: Miserable courses of life are the courses into which the soul is brought through the black, blue, and grey Lêsyâs.

l: happy courses of life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fourth Lecture.
s: Happy courses of life are the courses into which the soul is brought through the red, yellow, and white Lêsyâs.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fifth Lecture.
s: This unit concerns the Houseless Monk and the conduct required of a monk seeking liberation. It teaches that taking Pravragyâ requires renouncing attachments, possessions, building houses, cooking, fire, buying and selling, sensual desires, and praise. The monk should live simply, beg for alms without attachment, restrain his senses, and meditate on true things. At death, one who has rejected food, property, egoism, passions, and Âsravas becomes liberated from misery and reaches eternal beatitude.
The Houseless Monk follows the road shown by the wise ones, giving up house life and renouncing attachments. He lives without property, egoism, passions, and Âsravas, and reaches eternal beatitude.

The monk should abstain from killing, lying, stealing, carnal intercourse, desire, love, greed, building, cooking, lighting fires, buying, selling, and seeking praise or possessions. He should live in a pure and quiet place, beg for alms, restrain his senses and tongue, meditate on true things, and remain unattached until death.
Pravragyâ is taken when a sage gives up life in a house. In taking it, the sage should know and renounce the attachments that take hold of men.

A house may increase a monk's desire and passion through its pleasant furnishings and fragrances. A monk should not build a house or cause one to be built because living beings are killed during its construction.

l: Living Beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fifth Lecture.
s: Living beings, both movable and immovable, subtle and gross, may be killed when a house is built. Beings living in water, corn, earth, and wood are destroyed in the preparation of food and drink, and fire can destroy many beings.

l: food and drink, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fifth Lecture.
s: Food and drink may contain or destroy beings living in water, corn, earth, and wood. A monk should neither cook food and drink nor cause another to cook them.

l: buying and selling, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fifth Lecture.
s: Buying makes a monk a buyer, and selling makes him a merchant. A monk should not engage in buying and selling because it is a great sin.
A monk who lives on alms should beg rather than buy. Living on alms is described as benefitting, and the monk should collect alms in small parts while avoiding faults.
The monk should contentedly continue his begging-tour whether he receives alms or not.
A monk should have no property and should be indifferent to dirt and gold. He should not desire gold or silver or engage in buying and selling.
Following the road shown by the wise ones leads a monk to the end of all misery. At death, a monk who rejects food and leaves the human body is liberated from misery.

l: eternal beatitude, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Fifth Lecture.
s: A person without property, egoism, passions, and Âsravas obtains absolute knowledge and reaches eternal beatitude.

l: Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: The unit explains the division of Living Beings and Things without life for a monk who seeks self-control. Living Beings and Things without life make up the world (Lôka), while the Non-world (Alôka) contains only Things without life. Things without life are classified as formless things and things possessing form, and are described by substance, place, time, and development. Their development is considered through colour, smell, taste, touch, and figure.

l: Living Beings, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Living Beings, together with Things without life, make up the world (Lôka). Their division from Things without life is taught for the knowledge of a monk who exerts himself in self-control.

l: Things without life, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Things without life, together with Living Beings, make up the world (Lôka), while the Non-world (Alôka) contains only Things without life. They are divided into formless things and things possessing form, and are described with reference to substance, place, time, and development.
The world (Lôka) is made up of Living Beings and Things without life. Dharma and Adharma are co-extensive with it, while space fills it and the Non-world (Alôka).
The Non-world (Alôka) is the space where only Things without life are found. Space fills both the Non-world (Alôka) and the world (Lôka).

Time is one of the ten kinds of formless things and exists in what is called the place of time. Regarded as a continuous flow, it is without beginning and end; with regard to an individual thing, it has a beginning and an end.
Things without life are described with reference to development. Their development is fivefold, concerning colour, smell, taste, touch, and figure.

l: formless things, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Formless things are one of the two divisions of Things without life and are of ten kinds: Dharma, its divisions and indivisible parts; Adharma, its divisions and indivisible parts; space, its divisions and indivisible parts; and time.

l: things possessing form, Uttaradhyayana Sutra, Thirty-Sixth Lecture.
s: Things possessing form are one of the two divisions of Things without life and are of four kinds: compound things, their divisions, their indivisible parts, and atoms. Their longest duration is an immeasurable period and their shortest duration is one Samaya.
Dharma is one of the ten kinds of formless things, with its divisions and indivisible parts. It is co-extensive with the world (Lôka) and is ever without beginning and end.
Adharma is one of the ten kinds of formless things, with its divisions and indivisible parts. It is co-extensive with the world (Lôka) and is ever without beginning and end.
Space is one of the ten kinds of formless things, with its divisions and indivisible parts. It fills the world (Lôka) and the Non-world (Alôka), and is ever without beginning and end.
Colour is one of the five aspects of development. Things which develop with regard to colour are of five kinds: black, blue, red, yellow, and white.
Smell is one of the five aspects of development. Things which develop with regard to smell are of two kinds: sweet-smelling substances and substances of bad smell.
Taste is one of the five aspects of development. Things which develop with regard to taste are of five kinds: bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet.
